newsitem.title: IRAQ: Iraq denies obstructing U.N. helicopter flights.
newsitem.headline: Iraq denies obstructing U.N. helicopter flights.

text.p: Iraq denied on Wednesday it had obstructed flights by U.N. helicopters over its territory, saying such allegations were closer to science fiction than reality.

"There was no threat to the safety of the pilots of (U.N.) Special Commission or flights by their helicopters," the official Iraqi News Agency (INA) said, quoting a letter which Iraq's U.N. ambassador Nizar Hamdoun had sent to U.N. Security Council.

"What the Iraqis did was to protest against the use of a forbidden air route over a no-fly area (by U.N. arms inspectors) at a time when they had a shorter route at their disposal taking them to the civilian site they wanted to examine," Hamdoun said in his letter.

Council president Sergei Lavrov of Russia told reporters that chief U.N. arms inspector Rolf Ekeus had complained to the Security Council about Iraqi interference with U.N. helicopter flights during the inspection of several Iraqi facilities last week.
"We received a letter from the chairman of the Special Commission which will be discussed tomorrow when Mr Ekeus is coming to the council to brief us, hopefully," Lavrov said.

Ekeus heads the U.N. Special Commission (UNSCOM) in charge of scrapping Iraq's weapons of mass destruction. He told the council in his letter that four serious incidents had taken place in the past few days which had put the lives of U.N. helicopter crews at risk.

Ekeus said Iraqi air personnel accompanying the flights once threatened to shut off the helicopter's fuel pump and physically manhandled the U.N. chief air inspector and the U.N. commission's photographer to prevent them from taking photographs of the inspection site.

In another incident the Iraqi personnel grabbed the co- pilot's control stick, resulting in the abortion of the mission. In the other two incidents an accompanying Iraqi helicopter placed itself in the path of the U.N. aircraft, forcing them to take radical evasive action.

"These incidents are like those in science fiction films produced by Hollywood," Hamdoun said. "It is illogical for the Irqi personnel...to threaten the safety of UNSCOM's pilots because that will eventually endanger their own lives."
Hamdoun said UNSCOM and Iraq had agreed in June last year that the commission should respect Iraq's sovereignty. "It (UNSCOM) has to abide by this," he said.
Hamdoun did not say what facilities were included in the no- fly area in Tikrit 170 km (106 miles) north of Baghdad which Iraq has placed off bounds to U.N. flights.
